name: Lead White
poem: A soft, warm, deceptive white — the white of cathedral plaster, the powdered face of every queen, and the most quietly toxic colour ever loved.

recipe.note: A soft white carrying the faintest warm, creamy tint.

lenses.label: Art History
lenses.intro: Lead white was the only effective white available to oil painters for two thousand years — and arguably the single most important colour in the history of Western painting.

entries.title: Vermeer's Pearl
entries.blurb: The famous pearl is built up entirely from lead-white highlights — Vermeer's signature trick of suggesting depth with two perfectly placed dabs of opaque white.

entries.title: Caravaggio's Flesh
entries.blurb: The luminous skin of Caravaggio's figures is built layer by layer in lead white over a dark ground — the pigment's slight warmth makes flesh look lit from within.

entries.title: Rembrandt's Impasto
entries.blurb: Rembrandt's thick impasto highlights — the spotlit eye, the gold chain — depend on lead white's particular weight and texture, which no replacement quite matches.

lenses.label: Fashion
lenses.intro: For two and a half thousand years, lead white was the pigment of pale skin — applied directly to the face in pursuit of an ideal that destroyed the faces wearing it.

entries.title: Geisha Makeup
entries.blurb: The white-painted geisha face was lead white until the early 20th century — performers showed clear signs of lead poisoning by their thirties.

entries.title: Elizabethan Court
entries.blurb: Elizabeth I's signature "Mask of Youth" was Venetian ceruse — a paste of lead white and vinegar — applied so thickly her face was reportedly permanently scarred underneath.

entries.title: Victorian Lily Skin
entries.blurb: The Victorian ideal of pale, flawless skin sold millions of face powders containing lead white — banned in cosmetics in the U.S. only in 1938.

lenses.label: Nature
lenses.intro: Lead is a soft, silver metal that turns to white powder slowly in vinegar and air — a chemistry humans have exploited since the Bronze Age.

entries.title: Galena Ore
entries.blurb: The black, glassy ore that is the world's main source of lead — found in nearly every mining region and processed for both its lead and the small amount of silver it contains.

entries.title: Salt Flats
entries.blurb: The exact warm-white of lead-white pigment is the colour of large salt flats at midday — a flatness so complete it confuses the eye's depth perception.

entries.title: Bleached Coral
entries.blurb: When stressed coral expels its symbiotic algae, what's left is the white calcium carbonate skeleton — a lead-white-adjacent colour that signals dying ecosystems.

lenses.label: Pop Culture
lenses.intro: Lead white's quiet exit from modern life — replaced by titanium white in 1920s and banned in cosmetics by mid-century — is one of the great unsung public-health victories.

entries.title: Picasso's Complaint
entries.blurb: Picasso was reportedly horrified when titanium white replaced lead white in his usual paints — "it's no longer white, it's nothing" — the new pigment lacked lead's warmth.

entries.title: Banned 1978
entries.blurb: The U.S. banned lead-based house paint in 1978 — long after every other rich country, and long enough for several generations of children to be poisoned in their bedrooms.

entries.title: Conservation Headache
entries.blurb: Every museum's old-master painting has lead white in it — conservators wear masks and gloves to handle any surface that might be flaking. The risk is permanent.

lenses.label: Etymology
lenses.intro: Lead white's names trace its slow migration from chemistry to symbolism — from "corrosion of lead" to "the white of Saint John."

entries.title: "Cerussa"
entries.blurb: The Roman name — "cerussa" simply meant the powdered white that formed on lead exposed to vinegar fumes. Roman colourmen made it in clay pots stacked in dung-heaps.

entries.title: "Bianco di San Giovanni"
entries.blurb: "White of Saint John" — an alternative name from Florence, perhaps for the white linen St. John the Baptist wore. The pigment took on the saint's reputation for purity.

entries.title: "White Lead"
entries.blurb: When the colour merchant trade industrialised, the polite Latin names dropped away. "White lead" said what it was, and what was wrong with it, in two syllables.

lenses.label: Symbolism
lenses.intro: Lead white is the colour of every culture's fantasy of purity — and the chemistry of every culture's quiet poisoning by that fantasy.

entries.title: Purity
entries.blurb: The white wedding dress only became standard after Queen Victoria wore one in 1840 — and the bridal industry has been selling lead-white associations ever since.

entries.title: Beauty's Price
entries.blurb: Cosmetic lead poisoning was an open secret for centuries — physicians described it as "the disease of beautiful women," and prescribed more lead-white powder to mask the symptoms.

entries.title: Cleanliness
entries.blurb: Le Corbusier and the modernists demanded white walls for hygiene — a moral aesthetic descended directly from the lead-white interiors of the previous century.
